title: What happens when things collide
keyIdea: When a moving object hits another object, energy moves between them. The moving object slows down, and the object it hits starts moving, moves faster or changes shape. A rolling marble that hits a still marble of the same size almost stops, and the second marble rolls on. Faster objects have more energy, so they give a bigger push in a collision: a ball rolled from higher up a ramp moves a cup farther. Some energy always spreads out as sound, heating and changes of shape, which is why a crash goes bang and a clay ball does not bounce. Energy is never used up or destroyed; it only moves or changes form. A bumper or helmet that squashes makes the stop slower, so the push is gentler.
familyTip: Roll a ball into a stack of plastic cups or an empty box from close and then from far up a slope. Ask which roll pushed the box farther and why. Then drop a bouncy ball and a ball of play dough side by side and ask where the dough's energy went.

visual.caption: Where did the energy go? Drag each collision to a box, or tap it and then a box.

bins: Mostly into sound, heat or a dent
items: A marble hits a still marble
A cue ball hits a snooker ball
A football kicked into a net
A hammer hits a nail head and dents it

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pass energy from marble to marble, roll a ball into a cup from 3 heights, find where a crash's energy went, drop 3 balls, test bumpers.

kid: Anything that is moving has energy. When it hits something, some of that energy moves across. Roll a marble into a still marble of the same size. The first marble almost stops. The second marble rolls away. The energy passed from one to the other.

Faster things have more energy. Let a ball go from high up a ramp, and it is going fast at the bottom. It hits a paper cup and pushes it a long way. Start lower, and the ball is slower, so the cup moves less.

A crash is never quiet. You hear a bang. The bumper gets bent. The parts get a tiny bit warmer. Each one is energy going somewhere new. Energy is never used up. It just moves or changes into another kind.

Drop a bouncy ball and a clay ball. The bouncy ball springs back up. The clay ball goes splat and stays down. Its energy went into squashing it, warming it and making a thud. That is also why helmets have soft foam. The foam squashes, so the stop is slower and gentler.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. NGSS 4-PS3-3 asks pupils to predict the changes in energy that occur when objects collide, and 4-PS3-1 links an object's speed to its energy. In England, Year 5 forces covers the same experiences, though energy as a named idea comes later. At this age the goal is qualitative. Energy moves to the other object or spreads into sound, heating and changes of shape, and the total does not change.

The lab gives pupils evidence before the words. They roll a marble gently and hard into a still marble and watch it hand on its motion. They roll a ball from 10, 20 and 30 cm into a paper cup, where the model cup slides 6, 12 and 18 cm. They find four energy signs in a crash scene and ignore two that are not. They drop a bouncy ball, a tennis ball and clay from 1 metre and see 80, 55 and 0 cm. Last, they test bumpers that squash 0.2, 2 and 5 cm. All model numbers are typical values, not exact data.

Common mistakes. Many pupils say energy is used up or lost in a crash, rather than spread out into forms that are hard to see. Some think a heavier or faster object pushes less because it rushes past, or that a still object has energy. Some think two same-size marbles stick together or both stop. Others think a squashy bumper wastes energy, when it actually makes the stop gentler. Asking where the energy went, every time, fixes most of these.

practice.prompt: A marble rolls into a still marble of the same size, head-on. What happens?
choices: The first almost stops and the second rolls on
practice.hint: Think about where the moving energy goes.
practice.explain: The first marble passes almost all its moving energy to the second. It nearly stops, and the second rolls on.

practice.prompt: In a ramp test, the cup slid 6 cm when the ball started at 10 cm. If the slide grows in step with the start height, how many cm will it slide from {n}0 cm?
practice.hint: 10 cm gave 6 cm. How many lots of 10 cm is {n}0 cm?
practice.explain: {n}0 cm is {n} lots of 10 cm, so the slide is {n} × 6 = {=6*n} cm.

practice.prompt: Which shows energy turning into sound?
choices: A bang when two cars bump
practice.hint: Which of these would you hear? A collision that you can hear is turning energy into sound.
practice.explain: The bang is energy carried away as sound. Rolling quietly and a lamp shining are not collisions.

practice.prompt: A ball is dropped from 100 cm. It bounces back to {b} cm. How many cm short of 100 cm is it?
practice.hint: Take the bounce height away from 100.
practice.explain: 100 − {b} = {=100-b} cm. The energy for those missing centimetres went into sound and warming.

practice.prompt: Why does a clay ball not bounce?
choices: Its energy went into squashing and warming it
It has no energy when it falls
practice.hint: Look at its shape after it lands.
practice.explain: The clay changes shape and stays squashed. Its energy went into that change, a thud and warming. Energy is not destroyed.

pool.prompt: A ball rolls down a ramp from higher up. What happens when it hits a cup at the bottom?
pool.hint: Higher start, faster ball. What does speed tell you about energy?
pool.explain: A higher start makes the ball faster, and a faster ball has more energy to give the cup.

pool.prompt: After a car crash, where is the car's moving energy?
choices: In sound, heating and bent metal
pool.hint: Energy is never used up. Look for where it went.
pool.explain: The stopped car has no moving energy left. It went into the bang, warming and bending metal.

pool.prompt: A toy car has 10 units of moving energy. It hits a block. The block gets {a} units. How many units went into sound, heating and bending?
pool.hint: Energy is not lost, so all 10 units go somewhere.
pool.explain: 10 − {a} = {=10-a} units went into sound, heating and bending.

pool.prompt: Why do cycle helmets have a squashy foam layer?
choices: The foam squashes, so the stop is slower and gentler
The foam makes the helmet bounce off
pool.hint: What does the foam do when it is hit?
pool.explain: The foam squashes. The head slows over a longer time, so the push on it is smaller. The energy goes into squashing the foam.
The faster ball has more moving energy. A still ball has no moving energy.

pool.prompt: A bouncy ball dropped from 1 m bounces to 80 cm. What happened to the rest of its energy?
choices: It went into sound and warming
It stayed in the floor as speed
pool.hint: Energy cannot vanish. What did you hear?
pool.explain: The thud and a little warming carried away the rest. Energy changes form; it is never destroyed.

pool.prompt: A ball is dropped from {d}0 cm. It bounces back to half that height. How many cm high is the bounce?
pool.hint: Half of {d}0 is the same as {d}0 ÷ 2.
pool.explain: Half of {d}0 cm is {=5*d} cm. The other half of its energy went into sound and warming.

pool.prompt: A small marble hits a much heavier still ball. What is most likely?
choices: The small marble bounces back and the ball barely moves
The heavy ball shoots off fast
pool.hint: Is the heavy ball easy to move?
pool.explain: A heavy ball is hard to get moving. The small marble bounces back and only a little energy moves across.
